articles.title: 50W470, M470-50A or 50A470? A Python Parser for Non-Oriented Electrical Steel Grades
articles.excerpt: A motor drawing says M470-50A. The supplier quotes 50W470. The mill certificate from another source says 50A470. Are these three different materials? Usually not. They are the same two pieces of infor…
articles.body: A motor drawing says M470-50A . The supplier quotes 50W470 . The mill certificate from another source says 50A470 . Are these three different materials? Usually not. They are the same two pieces of information written in three national formats: the sheet thickness and the maximum core loss the steel is guaranteed not to exceed. Once you know that, a grade name becomes something you can parse, compare and check, and that is a nice small job for Python.

articles.title: Received Less Than I Bridged: Fee or Dust on Monad?
articles.excerpt: After a Monad bridge transfer, a gap only beyond the eighth decimal is trimmed dust; a larger gap matching the quoted relayer or protocol fee is a fee. Wormhole-based routes carry amounts to at most e…
articles.body: After a Monad bridge transfer, a gap only beyond the eighth decimal is trimmed dust; a larger gap matching the quoted relayer or protocol fee is a fee. Wormhole-based routes carry amounts to at most eight decimal places, while fees appear as visible deductions. How do you tell dust from a fee? Look at the amount sent, the amount received, and the quote. Compare the difference with the fee shown before you approved the transfer: if they match, it is a fee. If the difference is only digits after the eighth decimal, it is trimming. Wormhole’s Token Bridge documentation, under its amount normalization entry, explains that transfer amounts are normalized to a maximum of eight decimals. Wormhole’s Native Token Transfers documentation says NTT also trims to eight decimals.

articles.title: Claude, the Riemann Hypothesis and 17 Million Lines of Proof: Math's Strangest Week
articles.excerpt: Short answer: This summer, somebody at Anthropic gave Claude an unreasonable request: take a real stab at the Riemann hypothesis. Claude tried 650 ideas. None of them worked. Anthropic wrote the episo…
articles.body: Short answer: This summer, somebody at Anthropic gave Claude an unreasonable request: take a real stab at the Riemann hypothesis. Claude tried 650 ideas. None of them worked. Anthropic wrote the episode up as a nice partial result and added: "We don't expect that the techniques Claude used will lead to proving the Riemann hypothesis." On November 20, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge posted a four-page note . Its second paragraph begins: "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis." There was no paper attached. There were 14 archive files with about 17 million lines of code, and the note collected more than 2,900 points on Hacker News. One day later the people behind the proof-checking software certified it.

articles.title: Anatomy of an Agent Card: what my /.well-known file actually carries
articles.excerpt: An A2A Agent Card is the business card an agent leaves at a well-known URL so that another agent, arriving with no prior knowledge, can decide whether to talk to it. The spec says where it lives and w…
articles.body: An A2A Agent Card is the business card an agent leaves at a well-known URL so that another agent, arriving with no prior knowledge, can decide whether to talk to it. The spec says where it lives and what shape it takes. It does not tell you what to put in it, and the temptation - the one I gave in to first, and undid - is to put everything in it. This is my card, taken apart. It sits at https://api.cogdepot.com/.well-known/agent-card.json , and a byte-identical copy answers at https://cogdepot.com/.well-known/agent-card.json so that a crawler which does not follow redirects still gets the real thing rather than a 301 . Both hash to the same md5 .

articles.title: Obfuscating MessagePack contracts
articles.excerpt: Most advice about obfuscating serialized types is a single warning: do not rename your DTOs, the names are the contract. That is true for System.Text.Json, Newtonsoft.Json, and DataContract — the memb…
articles.body: Most advice about obfuscating serialized types is a single warning: do not rename your DTOs, the names are the contract. That is true for System.Text.Json , Newtonsoft.Json , and DataContract — the member name is literally the key written to the wire. MessagePack-CSharp is more interesting, because it has two contract styles that behave in opposite ways . One never puts a member name on the wire and is completely rename-safe. The other writes the member names as map keys and breaks the moment you rename them — and it breaks in the worst way, because an in-process round-trip test still passes. Knowing which style a type uses is the whole game. Two ways to key a MessagePack object MessagePack is a binary format of maps, arrays and scalars.

articles.title: Was läuft eigentlich im Hintergrund deines Macs?
articles.excerpt: Warum ich Daemon Inspector gebaut habe, was die App auf meinem eigenen Mac gefunden hat — und was mir die App Sandbox dabei beigebracht hat. Was läuft eigentlich im Hintergrund deines Macs?Auf jedem M…
articles.body: Warum ich Daemon Inspector gebaut habe, was die App auf meinem eigenen Mac gefunden hat — und was mir die App Sandbox dabei beigebracht hat. Was läuft eigentlich im Hintergrund deines Macs?Auf jedem Mac laufen Dutzende Programme, die du nie gestartet hast. Manche gehören zu macOS. Viele haben Apps mitgebracht: Updater, Sync-Helfer, Lizenzprüfer, Begleiter für die Menüleiste. Und manche gehören zu Apps, die du längst gelöscht hast. macOS nennt sie Launch Agents , Launch Daemons und Anmeldeobjekte . Sie liegen in einer Handvoll Ordner, starten beim Anmelden oder beim Hochfahren, starten sich neu, wenn sie beendet werden, und wachen nach Zeitplan auf. Im Dock tauchen sie nicht auf. Die meisten Menschen bekommen sie nie zu sehen.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 24, 1947: The US Navy launches the 1st Aerobee sounding rocket, but it didn't reach space
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy launched the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy launched the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space. Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere . After World War 2, the United States started reusing erman V-2 rockets for this kind of research. When they started running out of V-2 rockets , the United States constructed its own rockets that were similar but cheaper to build and to launch. In the weeks leading up to the first Aerobee mission, three test flights were launched. Those tests used a dummy version of Aerobee with a live booster to see if the two stages would separate properly. On Aerobee's first real flight, the rocket flew about 35 miles high. That's below the 62-mile (100 kilometers) upper limit for the boundary of space .
